text:
## Summary

**Data source overview.** This paper ("Learning Data-Driven Objectives to Optimize Interactive Systems") argues that interactive systems are conventionally optimized against hand-crafted objective functions that encode assumptions about user needs and therefore fail to reflect true user satisfaction. It formalizes user–system interaction as an MDP (user = agent, system = environment), recovers the hidden user reward function from observed interaction trajectories with Inverse Reinforcement Learning (MaxEnt-IRL, and DM-IRL as an oracle), and introduces the Interactive System Optimizer (ISO), which reformulates the system's transition distribution as a policy in a role-swapped MDP⁺ and iteratively optimizes it while users adapt. Simulations over 40 randomly sampled 64-state systems show significant, robust increases in expected state value, with degradation when state connectivity is high and trajectory diversity collapses.

**EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[78]**

*How the instruction set could be improved:* (a) The paper is a methods/optimization paper without explicit AI-safety framing — the instructions would benefit from explicit guidance on how to map "objective misspecification / proxy-objective" literature onto safety risk canonical names so that merging across 500k sources is stable (e.g., a controlled vocabulary or example canonical risk names such as "reward misspecification in learned objectives"). (b) Guidance is needed on whether negative/limitation findings (e.g., IRL degradation) should be validation-evidence nodes or new problem-analysis nodes that feed back into risks; I treated them as validation evidence with a feedback edge. (c) The rule "never create edges out of intervention nodes" conflicts with future-work items that are simultaneously limitations and proposals; clearer handling of "limitation → future-work intervention" chains would help. (d) A stated maximum node count per source (rather than a soft ratio) would reduce ambiguity.

**Inference strategy justification.** The paper states risks implicitly (misaligned handcrafted objectives, user inability to comprehend abrupt changes). I used light-to-moderate inference to (i) elevate "misalignment between handcrafted objectives and true user satisfaction" to a top-level risk node, (ii) derive monitoring and advanced-IRL interventions from the Results/Discussion diagnosis of MaxEnt-IRL deterioration, and (iii) derive the connectivity-constraint design intervention from the connection-factor findings. These inference-based edges carry confidence 1–2 and are flagged in their rationales.

**Extraction completeness.** All four sections of the causal chain are represented: risks (objective misalignment, user disorientation from abrupt change), problem analyses (unobservable experience, domain-knowledge dependence, complexity of user needs, indirect optimization, fixed environment, design constraints, homogeneous-user assumption), theoretical insights (trajectories encode latent rewards, MDP formalization, transition distribution as design variable, linear reward assumption, role-swap equivalence, user adaptation/convergence), design rationales, decomposed ISO mechanisms (MaxEnt-IRL, DM-IRL, MDP⁺ transformation, RL extraction of T*, soft value iteration, iterative loop), validation evidence (benchmark, oracle convergence, robustness to noise, connectivity degradation, diversity collapse), and eight interventions.

**Key limitations.** All evidence is simulation-based with synthetic one-hot state features and a single homogeneous user; no real deployment or human study exists, capping intervention maturity at 2. Figure-level numeric results were not available in text form, so validation node descriptions are qualitative. The framework's "ISO" name was deliberately decomposed into white-box component nodes.
